# Kinetics, closed-time field theory, and nonthermal scaling {#sec-kinetics-field-theory}

Hydrodynamics follows a few slow densities. Kinetic theory follows the
occupations of many propagating modes. Nonequilibrium field theory retains
response and fluctuations even when a quasiparticle occupation is not yet a
controlled description. These are complementary levels of approximation, and
understanding their relation prevents a formal calculation from silently
assuming the relaxation it is meant to explain.

We start from density-matrix evolution and elementary coherent states. We use
$\hbar=k_B=1$ and natural logarithms. A bosonic coherent state $|a\rangle$
is an eigenstate of an annihilation operator, $\hat a|a\rangle=a|a\rangle$.
Inserting coherent-state resolutions of the identity turns operator evolution
into an integral over complex fields. Fermions require Grassmann variables,
which anticommute; the contour logic is otherwise analogous.

## Why a nonequilibrium calculation has two time branches

For a state $\rho_0$, an expectation value is
$\operatorname{Tr}[U(t,0)\rho_0U(t,0)^\dagger O]$.
The density matrix evolves forward with $U$ and backward with $U^\dagger$.
Introduce independent sources on these two branches:

$$
Z[J_+,J_-]=\operatorname{Tr}
\left[U_{J_+}(t_f,0)\rho_0U_{J_-}(t_f,0)^\dagger\right].
$$ {#eq-kinetic-generating}

![The closed-time contour contains forward and backward evolution, sewn by the
trace at the final endpoint and by the initial density matrix at the initial
endpoint. This is an original conceptual diagram, not a simulated trajectory.](figs/keldysh-contour.png){#fig-kinetic-contour width=90%}

The contour travels from the initial time to $t_f$ and back. Its endpoints are
sewn together by the trace, while the initial density matrix supplies a boundary
condition. For equal sources, unitarity gives $Z[J,J]=1$. Functional derivatives
with respect to unequal sources generate correlation and response functions.

For a bosonic field with normal-ordered Hamiltonian function $H(a^*,a)$,
coherent-state time slicing gives the bulk action

$$
S=\int dt\,[a_+^*i\partial_ta_+-H(a_+^*,a_+)]
-\int dt\,[a_-^*i\partial_ta_--H(a_-^*,a_-)].
$$ {#eq-kinetic-contour-action}

The second integral has the opposite sign because the contour runs backward.
The weight is $e^{iS}$, multiplied by initial-state and endpoint factors.
Dropping those factors generally loses the initial occupations. A closed-time
contour avoids assuming an equilibrium imaginary-time preparation for a state
that was instead made by a quench.

This is the Schwinger–Keldysh construction. @berges2005nonequilibrium develops
its interacting quantum-field applications; @sieberer2016keldysh develops driven
open systems. The name denotes a bookkeeping framework, not a particular
weak-coupling approximation.

## Classical and quantum fields mean response coordinates

Define the Keldysh rotation

$$
a_{\mathrm{cl}}=\frac{a_++a_-}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 a_{\mathrm q}=\frac{a_+-a_-}{\sqrt2}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-rotation}

The field labeled “classical” is the branch average, and the “quantum” field is
the branch difference. These labels do not assert that either field has been
made classical. On identical forward and backward paths, $a_{\mathrm q}=0$
and the action cancels, as required by normalization.

For a free oscillator of frequency $\omega_0$, substitute the rotation into
the difference of the two quadratic actions. Terms containing only
$a_{\mathrm{cl}}$ cancel, and the result is

$$
S_0=\int dt\,
\left[a_{\mathrm q}^*(i\partial_t-\omega_0)a_{\mathrm{cl}}
+a_{\mathrm{cl}}^*(i\partial_t-\omega_0)a_{\mathrm q}\right]
+S_{\mathrm{boundary}}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-free-action}

Varying with respect to $a_{\mathrm q}^*$ gives the oscillator equation for
$a_{\mathrm{cl}}$. Thus a branch-difference field acts as a response variable.
The boundary contribution still fixes the initial fluctuation strength; the
absence of a bulk noise term does not mean that the vacuum has no fluctuations.

For a contact interaction $H_{\mathrm{int}}=g|a|^4/2$, substitution gives

$$
S_{\mathrm{int}}=-\frac g2\int dt\,
(|a_{\mathrm{cl}}|^2+|a_{\mathrm q}|^2)
(a_{\mathrm{cl}}^*a_{\mathrm q}+a_{\mathrm q}^*a_{\mathrm{cl}}).
$$ {#eq-kinetic-interaction}

Terms with one response field generate the nonlinear classical equation;
terms with three response fields encode additional quantum vertices.
Neglecting the latter is a *classical-statistical approximation*, useful for
suitably highly occupied modes with a correctly sampled initial distribution.
It can fail for low occupations, quantum scattering at late times, or ultraviolet
modes. A path-integral rewriting has not justified discarding them.

## Response, spectrum, and statistical fluctuations

For a bosonic mode define

$$
\begin{aligned}
G^R(t,t')&=-i\theta(t-t')\langle[\hat a(t),\hat a^\dagger(t')]\rangle,\\
G^A(t,t')&=i\theta(t'-t)\langle[\hat a(t),\hat a^\dagger(t')]\rangle,\\
G^K(t,t')&=-i\langle\{\hat a(t),\hat a^\dagger(t')\}\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kinetic-green-functions}

The retarded function describes causal propagation; the advanced function is
its adjoint counterpart; the Keldysh function records symmetrized fluctuations.
These are conventional Green-function signs. A physical susceptibility to a
Hamiltonian term $-fB$ has the sign derived explicitly in
@sec-linear-response; the source coupling determines that translation.
At equal times,
$n(t)=[iG^K(t,t)-1]/2$. The subtracted one is the bosonic vacuum contribution.
A *spectral function* is $A(\omega)=-2\operatorname{Im}G^R(\omega)$.
It describes where excitations can absorb or emit spectral weight; it is not an
occupation distribution.

For an equilibrium system, detailed balance relates fluctuations to spectrum:
$G^K(\omega)=[G^R(\omega)-G^A(\omega)]\coth(\beta\omega/2)$ for an
uncharged bosonic mode, with chemical potentials included as appropriate.
Out of equilibrium $G^K$ supplies independent information. Fitting a frequency
independent “effective temperature” from one ratio does not establish a thermal
state across all modes or frequencies.

## Worked example: a damped oscillator and its noise kernel

Take the explicitly Markovian master equation

$$
\dot\rho=-i[\omega_0a^\dagger a,\rho]
+2\kappa(n_B+1)\mathcal D[a]\rho
+2\kappa n_B\mathcal D[a^\dagger]\rho,
\quad
\mathcal D[L]\rho=L\rho L^\dagger-\tfrac12\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-damped-master}

Here $\kappa>0$ is the amplitude decay rate and $n_B$ the bath's resonant
occupation. Directly applying the adjoint generator gives
$\partial_t\langle a\rangle=-(i\omega_0+\kappa)\langle a\rangle$ and
$\dot n=-2\kappa(n-n_B)$.
The population therefore relaxes twice as fast as the amplitude.

In frequency space, the Gaussian Keldysh action has matrix

$$
S=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}
\begin{pmatrix}a_{\mathrm{cl}}^*&a_{\mathrm q}^*\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0&\omega-\omega_0-i\kappa\\
\omega-\omega_0+i\kappa&2i\kappa(2n_B+1)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a_{\mathrm{cl}}\\a_{\mathrm q}\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-damped-action}

The off-diagonal blocks encode retarded/advanced propagation. The imaginary
lower-right block makes $e^{iS}$ suppress large response-field fluctuations
and encodes noise. Inverting the block matrix yields

$$
G^R(\omega)=\frac1{\omega-\omega_0+i\kappa},\qquad
G^K(\omega)=\frac{-2i\kappa(2n_B+1)}
{(\omega-\omega_0)^2+\kappa^2}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-damped-greens}

Integrating $iG^K$ over frequency gives $2n_B+1$, reproducing the correct
stationary occupation. A Gaussian auxiliary noise can represent the
response-field quadratic term through a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation:
one introduces a random field whose Gaussian average reproduces that quadratic
weight. This connects Keldysh response/noise structure to Langevin descriptions.
The normalization depends on the $\sqrt2$ rotation and must be retained.

The Markov model takes $n_B$ constant near resonance. Its ratio
$G^K/(G^R-G^A)=2n_B+1$ approximates an equilibrium bath near $\omega_0$;
it does not satisfy the full frequency-dependent quantum thermal relation at
all frequencies. A bath approximation and exact equilibrium are distinct claims.

## How a kinetic equation emerges

In an interacting field theory, *self-energies* summarize corrections to free
propagation caused by interactions. Dyson equations for $G^R$, $G^A$, and $G^K$
can be reorganized into equations for spectral and statistical functions.
A *Wigner transform* Fourier transforms relative coordinates while retaining
their average:

$$
G(T,\omega)=\int d\tau\,e^{i\omega\tau}
G(T+\tau/2,T-\tau/2).
$$ {#eq-kinetic-wigner}

If average-time and average-position variation is slow compared with relative
correlation scales, a gradient expansion is possible. If the spectral function
also has a narrow peak, its weight defines a quasiparticle distribution
$f(\mathbf x,\mathbf k,t)$ with a group velocity.
Weak interactions, controlled factorization of multiparticle correlations,
and an appropriate Markov limit then produce

$$
\partial_tf+\mathbf v_{\mathbf k}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf x}f
+\mathbf F\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf k}f=I[f].
$$ {#eq-kinetic-boltzmann}

The logical order matters. Narrow quasiparticle peaks, slow gradients, and
short memory are assumptions to test, not identities following from the Wigner
transform. A far-from-equilibrium system can violate any of them.

The energy-conserving delta function in a collision integral has a simple
origin. A second-order interaction expansion contains an integral over the
relative duration of a collision,
$\int_0^\infty ds\,e^{i\Delta\epsilon s}
=\pi\delta(\Delta\epsilon)+i\,\mathcal P(1/\Delta\epsilon)$.
Its real part gives on-shell transition rates; its principal-value part shifts
energies. Extending the integration to infinity assumes a separation between
collision memory and the slow evolution of occupations. Close to a resonance
or strong-coupling regime, that separation can fail.

## Deriving conservation and entropy production of binary collisions

For elastic $1+2\leftrightarrow3+4$ scattering, write

$$
I_1=\int d2\,d3\,d4\,W_{12;34}
\left[f_3f_4(1+\eta f_1)(1+\eta f_2)
-f_1f_2(1+\eta f_3)(1+\eta f_4)\right].
$$ {#eq-kinetic-collision}

The label $i$ abbreviates momentum $\mathbf k_i$, $di=d^dk_i/(2\pi)^d$,
and $\eta=+1$ for bosons and $-1$ for fermions. Factors $1+f$ describe Bose
enhancement; factors $1-f$ describe Pauli blocking. The nonnegative rate kernel
$W$ includes the squared scattering amplitude, energy/momentum delta functions,
and symmetry factors in a consistent convention. Assume exchange symmetry
within each pair and microscopic reversibility
$W_{12;34}=W_{34;12}$.

Call the loss product $X$ and gain product $Y$, so $I_1=\int W(Y-X)$.
For any one-particle function $\phi$, symmetrizing over the four labels gives

$$
\int d1\,\phi_1I_1
=\frac14\int d1\,d2\,d3\,d4\,W
(\phi_1+\phi_2-\phi_3-\phi_4)(Y-X).
$$ {#eq-kinetic-invariant}

For $\phi=1$, $\mathbf k$, or $\epsilon_{\mathbf k}$, the first factor
vanishes on the collision shell. Binary scattering therefore conserves particle
number, momentum, and energy. This is also an implementation test: a numerical
collision discretization that drifts in these invariants is not trustworthy
merely because its occupations become smooth.

The entropy per mode is
$s_\eta(f)=\eta(1+\eta f)\ln(1+\eta f)-f\ln f$.
Its derivative is $s_\eta'(f)=\ln[(1+\eta f)/f]$.
Use this derivative as $\phi$ in the symmetrization above. The first factor
becomes $\ln(Y/X)$, hence

$$
\dot S=\frac14\int d1\,d2\,d3\,d4\,W
(Y-X)\ln\frac YX\geq0.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-h-theorem}

The inequality follows because the logarithm is increasing. It is an entropy
production theorem for the kinetic closure, not for exact closed-system
von Neumann entropy. Factorizing collision partners and neglecting memory have
discarded correlations. Detailed balance $X=Y$ admits
$f=[e^{\beta(\epsilon-\mu-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf k)}-\eta]^{-1}$,
with drift velocity multiplier $\mathbf u$. Additional collision invariants can
prevent this family from being the unique stationary manifold.

## A revealing failure: identical particles in one dimension

For quadratic dispersion in one dimension, energy and momentum conservation
imply
$k_1+k_2=k_3+k_4$ and $k_1^2+k_2^2=k_3^2+k_4^2$.
The sum and product of the two outgoing momenta equal those of the incoming
momenta. Thus $\{k_3,k_4\}=\{k_1,k_2\}$.
The gain and loss products cancel: this elastic binary collision integral cannot
redistribute an arbitrary momentum distribution.

Thermalization then requires other processes or ingredients, such as distinct
species, lattice kinematics, higher-body scattering, or integrability breaking.
This is a concrete bridge to GHD: integrable one-dimensional scattering changes
trajectories while preserving rapidities. Inserting a generic relaxation-time
term would add physics absent from the original integrable Hamiltonian.
The 2026 analysis @santra2026crossover studies such terms as an explicit
approximation for nearly integrable systems, with the preserved charge manifold
specified rather than assumed.

## Nonthermal fixed points and scaling constraints

Far from equilibrium, a distribution can approach a self-similar evolving form
rather than immediately becoming thermal:

$$
f(t,\mathbf k)=\left(\frac t{t_0}\right)^\alpha
f_S\!\left[\left(\frac t{t_0}\right)^\beta\mathbf k\right].
$$ {#eq-kinetic-selfsimilar}

A *nonthermal fixed point* is a scaling regime in which the rescaled function
$f_S$ becomes approximately time independent and insensitive to a range of
initial conditions. Positive $\beta$ shifts characteristic momentum toward the
infrared; negative $\beta$ shifts it toward the ultraviolet. This is a finite
scaling regime, not necessarily the final $t\to\infty$ state.

Change variables to $\mathbf q=t^\beta\mathbf k$. Particle number in the
scaling region behaves as $N_S\propto t^{\alpha-d\beta}$.
For dispersion $\epsilon\propto k^{z_{\mathrm{disp}}}$, its energy behaves as
$E_S\propto t^{\alpha-(d+z_{\mathrm{disp}})\beta}$.
Therefore

$$
\alpha=d\beta\quad\text{for conserved scaling-region particles},
\qquad
\alpha=(d+z_{\mathrm{disp}})\beta
\quad\text{for conserved scaling-region energy}.
$$ {#eq-kinetic-scaling-constraints}

A single nontrivially moving distribution cannot satisfy both conditions with
finite convergent integrals and $z_{\mathrm{disp}}>0$. Flux between distinct
momentum regions, an additional scale, or a breakdown of the ansatz is required.
This explains why *dual cascades*, simultaneous transport of particles and
energy toward different scales, arise naturally. A cascade is a sustained flux
through momentum scales; it need not involve a spatial current.

Power counting a collision term supplies another relation, but it depends on
the effective interaction. For nonrelativistic contact scattering with quadratic
dispersion, constant matrix element, and highly occupied modes, a local
four-wave collision integral scales as
$I\sim k^{2d-2}f^3$.
The gain/loss terms of fourth order in $f$ cancel, leaving cubic terms.
Under @eq-kinetic-selfsimilar, matching $\partial_tf$ to $I$ gives
$\alpha-1=3\alpha-(2d-2)\beta$.
Combining this naive bare-collision scaling with particle conservation gives
$\beta=-1/2$, rather than a positive infrared transport exponent. This is a
warning about assumptions: infrared nonthermal regimes can require a
scale-dependent effective scattering amplitude, nonperturbative resummation,
or defect dynamics. One cannot obtain their exponents by choosing a desired
scaling direction and applying an incompatible bare kinetic equation.

## Experiments, controlled approximations, and research projects

The experiments @prufer2018universal and @erne2018universal observe scaling
windows and compare different initial preparations in spinor and one-dimensional
Bose gases. Their strength lies in measured collapse and loss of initial-detail
sensitivity over an accessible range. Their finite time and momentum windows
must remain part of the claim. A faithful reproduction begins with unscaled
correlations, fits $\alpha$ and $\beta$ jointly, varies the chosen window, and
checks the scaling-region conserved quantity.

@schmied2019fixed connects nonperturbative kinetics, low-energy effective
fields, and topological defects. A controlled large-$N$ expansion uses the
inverse number of field components as an organizing parameter; a two-particle
irreducible effective action resums selected diagram classes self-consistently.
Neither name guarantees accuracy at arbitrary $N$ or coupling. Conservation,
cutoff dependence, and comparison with an independently controlled limit remain
necessary checks.

An emerging 2026 connection is the rare-fluctuation physics in
[@mcculloch2026coherence]: linearized fields can miss charge voids that protect
coherence. Its random-circuit construction and phenomenological deterministic
extension distinguish what can be derived from a microscopic model from what
is proposed as a broader mechanism. Combining ordinary kinetic relaxation,
nonlinear hydrodynamic large deviations, and genuinely quantum coherence is an
open research direction.

## Exercises and selected solutions

1. Perform the Keldysh rotation of a quadratic oscillator action and verify the
   cancellation of its classical–classical bulk term.
2. Invert @eq-kinetic-damped-action, integrate the resulting fluctuation spectrum,
   and check the stationary oscillator occupation.
3. Derive @eq-kinetic-invariant by explicitly exchanging the four collision labels.
   Identify which symmetry is needed at each exchange.
4. Derive the kinetic entropy inequality for fermions, including the domain
   $0\leq f\leq1$, and characterize when equality can hold.
5. Prove the one-dimensional binary-collision obstruction and explain why it
   invalidates a generic thermalizing Boltzmann ansatz for this setting.
6. Generate synthetic self-similar spectra with an imposed ultraviolet cutoff.
   Fit scaling exponents while changing the fitting range. Show how an omitted
   particle flux can mimic a violation of @eq-kinetic-scaling-constraints.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution: damped-oscillator fluctuations"}
The block inverse gives $G^K=-G^R[2i\kappa(2n_B+1)]G^A$.
Since $\int d\omega\,2\kappa/[2\pi((\omega-\omega_0)^2+\kappa^2)]=1$,
$iG^K(t,t)=2n_B+1$. Thus the measured occupation is
$[iG^K(t,t)-1]/2=n_B$. Dropping the vacuum one would incorrectly assign
half a particle to a zero-temperature oscillator.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution sketch: binary kinematics"}
Let $s=k_1+k_2=k_3+k_4$. Energy conservation implies
$s^2-2k_1k_2=s^2-2k_3k_4$, so the products agree too.
Both momentum pairs are roots of the same polynomial
$z^2-sz+k_1k_2=0$; they are identical up to permutation. Therefore $X=Y$
pointwise in the elastic collision integral for a single identical species.
The obstruction is kinematic, not a numerical failure to reach equilibrium.
:::
